extracted.intended_audience: 17th-century natural philosophers, mathematicians, astronomers, anatomists, and readers of the Philosophical Transactions
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and reporting first-hand natural-history, astronomical, anatomical, geological, and mathematical observations for a learned scientific journal: include precise measurements, dated chronologies, comparisons to prior authorities, and cautious interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical treatise: define images and judge appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘he propounds some theorems, from which the chief symptoms of refracted rays do result, their interjections and limits are easily discernible; the appearing places or images of such points are defined, both in regard to an eye situated in the axis of the radiation, and in regard to one placed elsewhere.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include theorems leading to observable symptoms of refracted rays; determine limits and intersections; define apparent places/images for different eye positions; provide determinations of places in the axis of the images for each kind of lens; give worked examples so the material is ‘ready, and serviceable to practise.’ Also treat accompanying phenomena (nature of light, colours, rainbows, prisms) and show how plain objects yield images and how they may be delineated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical lectures: scope and methods to include
rubrics_metrics.description: Lectures treat the nature of time in mathematical suppositions; mathematical hypotheses about simple motions (progressive and circular); method of indivisibles; generation of magnitudes by composition and concourse of motions; general theorems on tangents of curve lines; an analytical method of determining tangents extending to all sorts of curve lines; the nature and constitution of equations with roots and limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mathematical lecture/treatise should: address foundational concepts (time, motion hypotheses); present general methods (e.g., indivisibles, analytical tangent methods) applicable to many curves; include preparatory lemmata and general theorems; supply appendices with demonstrations by reduction ad absurdum where useful; give examples (conical sections, spirals, quadratrices) and demonstrate rules for dimensions of magnitudes and surfaces. Provide corollaries and supplementary notes valuable to mathematical readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volcanic eruption report completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The author ‘gives a short topography of this mountain, delivers a succinct relation both of the old and later eruptions, as also of this last fire of Etna, and assigns the perpendicular height of the same’ and then describes in detail the beginning (date), accompanying earthquakes, rents in the ground, noises, smoke, ejected molten stones, flows overwhelming towns, ash distribution, collapse of the summit and formation of a cauldron, measurements of ejected blocks, human interventions diverting flows, and duration until cessation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete eruption report should include: topography and height estimates (with comparison to other authorities), precise chronology (dates), seismic accompaniment, physical measurements (length/width of rents, size and distances of ejected blocks), descriptions of flow behavior and effects on towns/vegetation, distribution of ash (distances and directions), empirical corroborating experiments/observations (e.g., visual confirmation from summit), accounts of human mitigation efforts and their methods, and follow-up observations of heat/fumes after cessation; close with speculations and reasoned remarks on causes and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eclipse observation reporting standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations give times, altitudes, and corrected altitudes (after subtracting refraction), observer name and location, and calculations such as the middle time of eclipse: examples include reporting ‘the emersion: altitude of the crescent's upper edge’, ‘end of the eclipse: altitude of Arcturus’, correcting for refraction, and computing mid-eclipse times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record observer and precise location; note measured altitudes of lunar features and reference stars; apply and report corrections (e.g., refraction); provide times with minutes and seconds where possible; compute and state derived quantities (middle of eclipse); compare multiple observers' results and reconcile differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anatomical dissection reporting (porpoise example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dissection includes precise external measurements (length, girth), detailed description of external morphology (fins, skin, tail), internal anatomy (fat/blubber, muscular flesh, gut length and structure, stomach composition, liver, pancreas, spleen, kidneys, bladder, reproductive organs, diaphragm, heart, lungs, windpipe, larynx, cranial structure, nerves), and counts (teeth). The author notes omissions in prior descriptions and compares with earlier authorities (e.g., Rondeletius, Aristotle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide exact measurements and proportions; describe tissue types and their textural/functional properties; enumerate and locate organs and give comparative anatomy with other taxa (quadrupeds, dolphins); report unusual findings and where previous descriptions omitted features; offer reasoned hypotheses for organ function (e.g., uses of blubber) grounded in observation; include specimen provenance and circumstances of capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entomological/ichneumon observational reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports observe life-histories and behaviours: conjecture that ichneumon flies lay eggs in caterpillars, note that ichneumon maggots spin thecae and may produce swarms of ichneumones from a single caterpillar, describe nest-building, prey-carrying and burrowing behaviours of wasps, and report rearing outcomes or failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe observed behaviours in detail (egg-laying, larval development, theca construction, host interactions); give repeated observations and instances across species; attempt rearing or experimental checks (e.g., digging for buried hosts); state hypotheses cautiously when not absolutely demonstrated; note variations (some species feed young with captured prey, others may lay eggs in hosts); include natural-history context and comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petrified shells / fossil-evidence argumentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The correspondent argues about petrified shells in English quarries: he notes that quarry 'shells' have the same texture as surrounding rock (iron-stone, lime, spar), that different quarries yield different 'species' of shell-stones, and that he could not find matching living species on nearby shores or waters, therefore concluding they may be lapides sui generis rather than petrified animal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing about fossil origin, compare quarry specimens' material/texture with surrounding matrix; survey local shores, freshwaters, and fields for living analogues; compare across multiple quarry sites and stone types; avoid litigious contradiction—present alternative explanations and base conclusions on systematic comparative observation and distributional evidence.
